researchRequests.question: What is the actual end-to-end cycle time from pre-qualification to award for provincial emergency-response robot tenders in the last two years?
At what retail price do household service robot purchase intentions collapse in current consumer surveys, and how do platform subsidies shift that threshold?

counterparties.identity: Established rescue-robotics integrator holding provincial framework agreements
counterparties.coreInterest: Defend framework-agreement revenue and procurement relationships against a cheaper spherical entrant; keep certification requirements aligned with its own tracked platforms.
responseTools: Bundle discounts across its tracked-robot fleet inside existing framework agreements
Lobby certification bodies to add tracked-platform-biased field-test criteria
Accelerate tender timing with incumbent-friendly spec lock-in
constraints: 18-month internal hardware refresh cycle limits fast counter-launches
Recent field failures make aggressive public claims reputationally risky
Thin software team cannot quickly match autonomy features

counterparties.identity: Consumer smart-home platform vendor able to subsidize household robots
counterparties.coreInterest: Own the household entry point and its data; prevent an independent robot brand from establishing a direct consumer relationship.
responseTools: Subsidized hardware bundles tied to platform subscriptions
Exclusive supplier agreements with shared component vendors
constraints: No rescue or industrial certification track record
Hardware margin pressure caps subsidy depth per quarter
Antitrust scrutiny limits overt exclusivity enforcement

ourActions.description: Commit engineering and the remaining certification budget to one provincial emergency-bureau rescue pilot, targeting the next tender window.
Launch a household service configuration through consumer channels with tooling and initial inventory committed this quarter.
Defer market commitment for two quarters, keep the dual-use prototype line, and spend only on certification pre-study and demand probes.

responseMatrix.optimalResponse: Immediately lobby the certification body to insert tracked-platform field criteria and pre-announce a framework-agreement discount, raising our qualification cost before the tender opens.
responseMatrix.worstResponseForUs: Certification criteria amended to require multi-terrain track records we cannot show, excluding the spherical platform from the next two tender rounds.
responseMatrix.mostLikelyResponse: Quiet bundle discounts to the emergency bureau plus informal doubts about spherical-platform durability, without formal spec changes this cycle.
responseMatrix.responseWindow: 1-2 quarters, bounded by the published tender calendar
responseMatrix.optimalLikelyGap: The optimal lobbying play needs public attention on certification, which its recent field failures make risky; informal price and doubt tactics are cheaper and deniable.
responseMatrix.ourCounterResponse: Pre-file third-party field-test evidence with the bureau and lock a reference deployment letter before the tender publishes; budget already reserved in the pilot plan.
responseMatrix.fallbackCost: One extra field demonstration and roughly one month of schedule slack already inside the pilot budget envelope.

responseMatrix.optimalResponse: Publicly reframe us as a consumer toy vendor in procurement circles, cementing its rescue-market position without spending on price.
responseMatrix.worstResponseForUs: Procurement contacts treat our rescue ambitions as abandoned, closing warm channels we would need if we later re-enter rescue.
responseMatrix.mostLikelyResponse: No direct action beyond narrative positioning, since our household move exits its market.
responseMatrix.responseWindow: Within one quarter of a public consumer launch
responseMatrix.optimalLikelyGap: Optimal and likely nearly coincide because ignoring us while talking down our seriousness costs it nothing.
responseMatrix.ourCounterResponse: Maintain a minimal certification pre-study track and one bureau relationship to keep re-entry credible; costs one part-time liaison.
responseMatrix.fallbackCost: Part-time liaison plus annual certification pre-study fees, sustainable within current runway.

responseMatrix.optimalResponse: Accelerate the next tender and push spec lock-in now, closing the window while we are uncommitted.
responseMatrix.worstResponseForUs: Tender brought forward with incumbent-shaped specs, so waiting costs us the very cycle we were saving for.
responseMatrix.mostLikelyResponse: Continue business as usual; a quiet observer does not trigger its threat model.
responseMatrix.responseWindow: Tied to the annual tender calendar, roughly 2-4 quarters
responseMatrix.optimalLikelyGap: Accelerating tenders requires bureau cooperation it cannot unilaterally force, so the likely response is inaction.
responseMatrix.ourCounterResponse: Monitor tender pre-announcements weekly and keep a 6-week fast-follow pilot package ready; preparation cost only.
responseMatrix.fallbackCost: Maintaining the fast-follow package costs one engineer-week per month.

responseMatrix.optimalResponse: Ignore the rescue niche and lock shared component suppliers into priority contracts as insurance against our later consumer pivot.
responseMatrix.worstResponseForUs: Key drive-unit supplier capacity reserved by the platform, lengthening our lead times even for rescue units.
responseMatrix.mostLikelyResponse: No visible reaction; rescue procurement is outside its platform economics.
responseMatrix.responseWindow: 2-4 quarters, driven by its supplier contract renewal cycle
responseMatrix.optimalLikelyGap: Supplier lock-up costs real margin for a hypothetical threat, so the likely response is monitoring only.
responseMatrix.ourCounterResponse: Dual-source the drive unit and pre-book pilot-volume capacity; already priced into the pilot bill of materials.
responseMatrix.fallbackCost: Second-source qualification adds a bounded one-time engineering cost.

responseMatrix.optimalResponse: Launch a subsidized bundle at a price below our unit cost, tied to its subscription, timed to our channel launch.
responseMatrix.worstResponseForUs: A sustained subsidy war plus app-store demotion that our runway cannot outlast, stranding committed tooling and inventory.
responseMatrix.mostLikelyResponse: Targeted promotional pricing and preferential placement for its own bundle during our launch window, short of a full subsidy war.
responseMatrix.responseWindow: Within weeks of a public consumer launch
responseMatrix.optimalLikelyGap: Full subsidy war breaches its quarterly margin cap and invites antitrust attention, so it prefers targeted promotions first.
responseMatrix.ourCounterResponse: No credible counter within budget: matching subsidies breaches the funding hard constraint, and independent distribution cannot replace platform placement at launch volume.
responseMatrix.fallbackCost: Exiting after a failed launch strands tooling and inventory and consumes most remaining runway.

responseMatrix.optimalResponse: Pre-announce its own household robot roadmap to freeze consumer demand and deter our later entry.
responseMatrix.worstResponseForUs: Demand freeze plus supplier priority contracts make a later household entry structurally harder.
responseMatrix.mostLikelyResponse: Continue roadmap on its own schedule; an uncommitted observer does not justify pre-announcement risk.
responseMatrix.responseWindow: 1-2 quarters around its annual platform event
responseMatrix.optimalLikelyGap: Pre-announcing against a non-entrant risks osborning its current bundle sales, so silence is likelier.
responseMatrix.ourCounterResponse: Track its platform event announcements and re-run the household demand probe afterwards; monitoring cost only.
responseMatrix.fallbackCost: One demand-probe refresh per quarter, negligible against runway.

publicationTest.newInformationRevealed: Publication would reveal our 12-month runway ceiling, the rescue-first sequencing logic, and that we treat a platform subsidy war as unanswerable, giving the platform a cheap deterrence playbook.
publicationTest.mitigation: Keep runway figures and tender timing private; publish only capability demonstrations and already-observable pilot facts; refresh this matrix before any public launch commitment.

downsideAsymmetry.worstCase: Certification amendment excludes the spherical platform for two tender rounds after pilot spend is committed.
downsideAsymmetry.exitPath: Wind down the pilot after the tender decision, retain certification artifacts and field data for the dual-use prototype.
downsideAsymmetry.exitCost: Pilot budget minus reusable certification and field-test assets; no inventory exposure.

downsideAsymmetry.worstCase: Subsidy war plus channel demotion during launch quarter with tooling and inventory already committed.
downsideAsymmetry.exitPath: Fire-sale inventory through secondary channels and retool the line back to the dual-use prototype.
downsideAsymmetry.exitCost: Committed tooling, inventory write-down, and most remaining runway; recovery depends on salvage prices we do not control.

downsideAsymmetry.worstCase: Tender accelerates with incumbent-shaped specs and household demand is frozen by a platform pre-announcement in the same period.
downsideAsymmetry.exitPath: Activate the prepared fast-follow pilot package or pivot the demand probe into a niche vertical.
downsideAsymmetry.exitCost: Two quarters of calendar time and probe spending; core capital preserved.

content.reflexivityWarning: Adopting this matrix makes our tender-window behavior more predictable to anyone who infers it; a leak would hand the incumbent the certification-lobbying trigger and tell the platform that targeted promotions alone deter us. The likely-response estimates are themselves reflexive: any public move by us changes the counterparties' information sets, so this matrix must be re-run after each observable action rather than treated as a static forecast.
